opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tricky question, because chip design cycles are long. From when you start designing to when you have silicon in customers' hands, it's two or three years, maybe more. Meanwhile, the model architectures and workloads are changing every few months. So you're always betting on what the world will look like several years out.

I'd think about it in terms of what's likely to stay stable versus what's likely to change. Some things have been remarkably stable. Matrix multiplication is still the core of almost everything. Transformers have stuck around much longer than many people expected, and even the alternatives, like state space models or linear attention, still boil down to a lot of matmuls plus some memory-bound operations. So betting on fast matmul and high memory bandwidth is a pretty safe bet.

What's changed a lot is the balance between training and inference, and within inference, the shape of the workload. A couple of years ago most people thought about chatbots, short prompts and short responses. Now with reasoning models and agents, you're generating very long sequences, you have long contexts, you're doing a lot of decoding. Decoding is very memory-bandwidth bound, so the bottleneck shifts. If I were starting a chip company now, I'd think hard about inference, especially low-latency, long-context decoding, because that's where a lot of the compute is going and where the incumbents may not be perfectly optimized.

The other thing I'd say is, don't over-specialize. There's a real temptation to hardcode a particular architecture, say bake the transformer into silicon. That can give you a huge efficiency win if the bet is right, but if the field shifts, to a different attention variant, mixture of experts with different sparsity patterns, lower precision formats, whatever, you can get stranded. So you want enough programmability to adapt. Some of the most successful hardware has been specialized in the right places, like tensor cores for matmul, but flexible elsewhere.

And finally, software matters as much as hardware. A big part of why NVIDIA is so dominant is the ecosystem: CUDA, the libraries, the fact that researchers write kernels for it first. A startup with great hardware but a painful software story will struggle. So I'd invest heavily in making it easy for people to get their models running and running fast, and ideally work closely with a few customers whose workloads you deeply understand, rather than trying to be everything to everyone from day one.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on inference, especially long-context decoding, but it also advises against over-specializing and does not clearly recommend designing the chips around a concentrated bet on that workload.

r002.rationale: It notes NVIDIA’s software ecosystem advantage and suggests incumbents may be less optimized for certain workloads, but does not argue that incumbents will out-execute a startup optimizing for general workloads.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, partly because I've been on both sides of it. I work on the software side, on things like FlashAttention and Mamba, but I've also spent a lot of time talking to people building chips.

The fundamental problem is the timeline mismatch. If you start designing a chip today, it ships in maybe two to three years. And the workloads in AI change on a much faster cycle than that. So you're essentially trying to predict what people will want to run in 2028 or 2029. That's really hard. Four years ago people weren't sure transformers would even be the dominant architecture. Now there's this question of whether attention stays dominant, or whether things like state space models or hybrid architectures take over, or whether inference-time compute changes the whole profile of what you need.

So the way I'd think about it is: don't bet on a specific architecture. Bet on the primitives that are likely to survive. Matrix multiplication is going to be there. Some kind of memory bandwidth bottleneck is going to be there. Reductions, elementwise ops, some notion of moving data between chips efficiently. If you look at what actually constrains performance on modern hardware, it's increasingly memory and communication, not raw FLOPs. That's been true for a while and I think it continues to be true. So if you're going to over-invest somewhere, over-invest in memory bandwidth and interconnect rather than in one particular dataflow pattern.

The second thing I'd say is that the software story matters as much as the hardware. NVIDIA's advantage isn't just the silicon. It's that when a new architecture shows up, someone can write a kernel for it in a weekend and it just works. A lot of chip startups have built hardware that's great for one specific workload, but the moment the workload shifts a little bit, the compiler can't keep up and all that peak performance is unreachable. So I'd want flexibility, programmability, and a really good story for how a researcher gets a new idea running on the chip without waiting six months for your team to write the kernel.

And then the third thing is just being honest about which part of the market you're going after. Training and inference have really diverged. Inference, especially with these long reasoning traces, is dominated by decoding, which is memory-bound, small-batch, latency-sensitive. Training is more about throughput and scale-out. If you try to do both you'll probably do neither well as a startup. Picking one and being really good at it is a much more defensible position than trying to be a general-purpose GPU competitor.

So I guess the short version is: bet on the bottlenecks, not on the model. Make the thing programmable enough that you can adapt when you're wrong, because you will be wrong about something. And pick a lane.

r001.rationale: The response recommends betting on durable primitives rather than a specific future workload or architecture. Picking a market lane does not communicate a concentrated bet on a future dominant workload.

r002.rationale: The response describes NVIDIA’s software advantage and says startups trying to serve both training and inference may do neither well. It does not argue that incumbents will out-execute a startup for optimizing general workloads.

astra-6.text:
I think the hard part is that designing a chip takes years, and the workloads can change a lot in that time. You could build something that’s extremely good at today’s model and then discover that the bottleneck has moved by the time you ship.

So I would start by asking which properties of the workload are likely to persist. Matrix multiplication is probably a fairly robust bet. Moving data efficiently is another one. Betting on one particular attention formulation or one particular model architecture is much riskier. You want enough flexibility that you can adapt without giving up all the efficiency that makes custom hardware attractive.

And I’d make the software part of that bet from day one. Can someone implement a new operation efficiently? Can they get their model running without spending six months rewriting it? Peak performance matters, but the ability to reach that performance on a changing workload matters just as much.

Ideally, you’re working closely with people building models, testing your assumptions continuously. You won’t predict everything correctly. The goal is to build something that’s still useful when some of your predictions are wrong.

r001.rationale: It recommends durable workload properties and flexibility, and warns against betting on one model architecture or attention formulation. It does not recommend concentrating the chip design on one future dominant workload.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that incumbents will out-execute a startup focused on general workloads.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hard part is that you’re designing hardware for workloads that might look quite different by the time the chip ships. So I’d be cautious about taking today’s most popular model and making that run really, really fast at the expense of everything else.

You want to ask: what’s likely to stay the same? We’ll probably still need a lot of matrix multiplication, we’ll still need to move data efficiently, and memory bandwidth and communication will still matter. But the exact shapes, the balance between those operations, and even the model architecture can change.

So I’d start with those durable constraints, then work closely with people building models. And I’d invest heavily in the software stack, because that’s what lets you adapt when the workload changes. There’s a tradeoff: you need enough specialization to have a compelling advantage, but enough flexibility that one algorithmic change doesn’t invalidate your whole bet.

r001.rationale: The response advises against betting the chip on one popular model and favors durable constraints with flexibility; it does not recommend concentrating on a future dominant workload.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim incumbents would out-execute a startup pursuing general workloads.
